title: A 'routine day' that unravelled into tragedy
article: The deadly and devastating eight-minute interaction between a police officer and suspect Ryan Dube is the focus of a coroner's inquest that began this week in Niagara Falls, a legal hearing aimed at preventing similar deaths.

The Ontario coroner's office is looking into the 2012 death of Dube, an 18-year-old man, who fell to his death in the Niagara gorge after running from Niagara Regional Police Const. Jacob Smits, who was trying to arrest him. A 30-second chase resulted in both men falling approximately 30 metres into the gorge. Dube died as a result of the fall, and Smits suffered what the coroner's counsel called "life-threatening injuries."

The purpose of the inquest is to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths in similar situations in the future, said Dr. Jack Stanborough, the presiding coroner. A death while someone is in police custody is one three circumstances in which an inquest is held automatically, he said.

"We are not here to point fingers or lay blame," Stanborough told the five-member jury on Monday, the first day of the inquest at the Americana Conference Resort and Spa. "If your recommendations are reasonable and responsible, they may prevent similar deaths in similar situations in the future."

Dube's death started on a "routine day" that "quickly unravelled into a tragic situation," Graeme Leach, counsel for the Ontario coroner's office, said at the start of the inquest being held in a conference room at a Niagara Falls hotel. It's scheduled to last 10 days and hear from 15 witnesses, including police officers, firefighters and paramedics who rushed to the aid of both Dube and Smits.

Dube died on July 24, 2012 after he fell into the Niagara gorge. He was running away from Smits who flagged him down near the corner of Ontario Avenue and Otter Street. At 5 p.m., an hour before the end of his shift, Smits got the call to carry out an arrest warrant issued earlier in the day for an alleged breach of Dube's probation terms.
"Did I feel like I had to chase him? Yes, I did," Smits testified Monday.

Smits said he was parked a few blocks from a youth shelter where Dube was known to live, waiting for a backup officer to arrive before they moved in for the arrest. Suddenly, Dube and a female friend appeared on the sidewalk in front of Smits' cruiser.
"It would almost be a neglect of duty to let someone wanted on an arrest warrant to walk away from you," Smits testified.

Smits, a three-year veteran of the NRP at the time, said he got out of his car and called Dube over for a chat. The officer told the suspect he would be arrested but allowed him to smoke a cigarette before taking him. Smits told the inquest he engaged his suspect in conversation to give the backup officer time to arrive and to de-escalate what he feared would turn into a physical fight if he tried to apprehend Dube on his own.

When Smits reached into his police car to get a business card for Dube's friend, Dube ran. He ran down Ontario Avenue, but Smits got his police car to follow. When he ran across a city park, Smits followed. Smits got out of his car when he drove into an obstacle and couldn't drive any further.

When Smits heard tree branches rustling, he concluded Dube had hopped over a stone wall that separated a public sidewalk from at rocky era at the top of the Niagara gorge. Smits called out to him to stop because he was close to going over the edge.

Smits jumped over the wall himself in a bid to stop Dube from falling. "His eyes got as big as saucers. He started to fall and there's nothing he can do to stop this... . My thought process was grab a tree, grab him, hold on," Smits said. From the time Smits flagged Dube down to the time they tumbled down the gorge, they had been in contact for eight minutes. The chase was estimated to have lasted just 30 seconds.

Smits was also "severely injured" in the fall, Leach said. Smits recounted a list of injuries, including a broken pelvis, femur, hip bone and ankle. He was hospitalized for six weeks, spent months in physiotherapy and still has rods and plates in his body. A doctor only cleared him to return to police work in December 2013, nearly a year and a half after the incident.

A Special Investigations Unit investigation said there were no grounds to charge Smits with any criminal charges. The SIU is the independent body that investigates whether charges should be laid when civilians die or are injured during contact with police.

Lawyers representing Dube's family, the Niagara Regional Police board, the Niagara Parks Commission, the fire department and Niagara's paramedic service have standing at the inquest, meaning they'll have the opportunity to question the 15 witnesses expected to be called.
